questions.problem: In summer, the daily maximum temperature in a particular city (rounded to the nearest degree) varies between ${25}^{∘}C$ and ${36}^{∘}C,$ inclusive. Assuming that each maximum temperature value has the same probability of occurring on a given summer day, what is the expected value of the daily maximum temperature?
questions.worked_solution:
Let $X$ represent the daily maximum temperature (rounded to the nearest degree) on a randomly selected day. From the problem statement, we know that $X∼U\{25,26,…,36\},$ and we wish to compute $\text{E}[X].$

In general, if $X∼U\{a,a+1,…,b\},$ then $X$ has the following expected value:

$$
\text{E}[X]=\frac{a+b}{2}
$$

So, for our random variable $X∼U\{25,26,…,36\},$ we have the following expected value:

$$
\text{E}[X]=\frac{25+36}{2}=30.5
$$

Therefore, the expected value of the maximum temperature is ${30.5}^{∘}C.$

questions.problem: A traditional festival is usually held on a single day after the $6$th and before the $15$th of September. The exact day is selected each year and depends on the weather conditions. Assuming that each day after the $6$th and before the $15$th of September has the same probability of being chosen, what is the standard deviation of the selected days? Round your answer to $2$ decimal places.
questions.worked_solution:
Let $X$ represent the date of the selected day. From the problem statement, we know that $X∼U\{7,8,…,14\},$ and we wish to compute $\text{SD}[X].$

In general, if $X∼U\{a,a+1,…,b\},$ then the variance of $X$ is

$$
\text{Var}[X]=\frac{|S{|}^{2}-1}{12}
$$

where $S=\{a,a+1,…,b\}.$

Now, we know that

$$
\begin{aligned}|S| & =b-a+1 \\  & =14-7+1 \\  & =8.\end{aligned}
$$

So, for our random variable $X∼U\{7,8,…,14\},$ we have the following variance:

$$
\text{Var}[X]=\frac{{8}^{2}-1}{12}=\frac{63}{12}
$$

Finally,

$$
\text{SD}[X]=\sqrt{\frac{63}{12}}≈2.29.
$$

canonical_examples.name:
Example: 
                    Computing Mean Values in Context
canonical_examples.problem: A fair die has $12$ sides labeled with numbers $1$ through $12.$ What is the expected value of a random roll of this die?
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Let $X$ represent the number the die lands on. From the problem statement, we know that $X \sim U \{1, 2, \ldots, 12\},$ and we wish to compute $\textrm E[X].$

In general, if $X \sim U \{a, a + 1, \ldots, b\},$ then $X$ has the following expected value:

$$
\textrm E[X] = \dfrac{a+b}{2}
$$

So, for our random variable $X \sim U \{ 1, 2, \ldots, 12\},$ we have the following expected value:

$$
\textrm E[X] = \dfrac{1+12}{2} = 6.5
$$

Therefore, the expected value is $6.5.$

canonical_examples.name:
Example: 
                    Computing Variances in Context
canonical_examples.problem: A fair die has sides labeled with numbers $4$ through $15.$ What is the variance of the numbers obtained when rolling this die?
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Let $X$ represent the number the die lands on. From the problem statement, we know that $X \sim U \{ 4, 5, \ldots, 15 \},$ and we wish to compute $\textrm{Var}[X].$

In general, if $X \sim U \{a, a + 1, \ldots, b\},$ then the variance of $X$ is

$$
\textrm{Var}[X] = \dfrac{|S|^2-1}{12}
$$

where $S = \{a, a+1, \ldots, b\}.$

Now, we know that

$$
\begin{aligned}|S| & =b-a+1 \\  & =15-4+1 \\  & =12.\end{aligned}
$$

So, for our random variable $X \sim U \{ 4, 5, \ldots, 15 \},$ we have the following variance:

$$
\textrm{Var}[X] = \dfrac{12^2 - 1}{12} = \dfrac{143}{12}
$$

Therefore, the variance is $\dfrac{143}{12}.$

tutorials.name: Introduction
tutorials.problem:
We know that if a random variable $X$ follows a *discrete* uniform distribution, then it has the following probability mass function:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14211555/assets/0abfcf5eccaaaf22dbc144f58098d394297a5819a1857ff316ce9e9d01e44f7d.svg)

Let's now suppose that 

$$
X\sim U\{a, a+1, a+2, \ldots, b\},
$$

where $a$ and $b$ are integers. In other words, we're concerned with the special case where the support $S$ of $X$ contains every integer between $a$ and $b$ inclusive. 

In this case, it can be shown that the mean value of $X$ is given by

$$
\textrm{E}[X] = \dfrac{a+b}{2}.
$$

It can also be shown that

$$
\textrm{Var}[X] = \dfrac{|S|^2-1}{12}.
$$

We'll prove these results at the end of the lesson.

tutorials.name: Proving the Formula for the Mean
tutorials.problem:
Here, we will show that for $X\sim \{a, a+1, a+2, \ldots, b\},$ we have

$$
\textrm{E}[X] = \dfrac{a+b}{2}.
$$

First, recall that the probability mass function of $X$ is given by

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14211555/assets/36e73322640df22386428fdc41d1940ef7469587566c2f4f24936158292c087c.svg)

By the definition of expected value for discrete random variables, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[X] & ={\sum }_{x\in S}xf(x) \\  & ={\sum }_{x\in S}x\cdot \frac{1}{|S|} \\  & =\frac{1}{|S|}{\sum }_{x\in S}x \\  & =\frac{1}{|S|}[a+(a+1)+(a+2)+⋯+b].\end{aligned}
$$

Now, the term in the square brackets is an arithmetic series with the first term $a$ and the last term $b.$ Therefore, using the formula for the sum of an arithmetic series, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[X] & =\frac{1}{|S|}[a+(a+1)+(a+2)+⋯+b] \\  & =\frac{1}{|S|}\cdot \frac{|S|}{2}\cdot (a+b) \\  & =\frac{1}{\cancel{|S|}}\cdot \frac{\cancel{|S|}}{2}\cdot (a+b) \\  & =\frac{a+b}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

as required.

tutorials.name: Proving the Formula for the Variance
tutorials.problem:
Let's now show that for $X\sim \{a, a+1, a+2, \ldots, b\},$ we have

$$
\textrm{Var}[X] = \dfrac{|S|^2-1}{12}.
$$

We will assume, without loss of generality, that the distribution of our random variable $X$ is given by

$$
X\sim\{1, 2, 3, \ldots, |S|\}.
$$

We do not lose generality here because, in general, the variance (i.e., spread) of a random variable is unaffected by translations:

$$
\textrm{Var}[X + c] = \textrm{Var}[X]
$$

  

By the definition of $\textrm{E}[X^2],$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[{X}^{2}] & ={\sum }_{x\in S}{x}^{2}f(x) \\  & ={\sum }_{x\in S}{x}^{2}\cdot \frac{1}{|S|} \\  & =\frac{1}{|S|}\cdot {\sum }_{x\in S}{x}^{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{|S|}\cdot [{1}^{2}+{2}^{2}+⋯+|S{|}^{2}].\end{aligned}
$$

We now make use of the following result:

$$
\sum_{i=1}^n i^2 = \dfrac16 n (n+1)(2n+1)
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[{X}^{2}] & =\frac{1}{|S|}\cdot [{1}^{2}+{2}^{2}+⋯+|S{|}^{2}] \\  & =\frac{1}{|S|}\cdot \frac{1}{6}\cdot |S|\cdot (|S|+1)(2|S|+1) \\  & =\frac{1}{\cancel{|S|}}\cdot \frac{1}{6}\cdot \cancel{|S|}\cdot (|S|+1)(2|S|+1) \\  & =\frac{(|S|+1)(2|S|+1)}{6}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we use the following results:

$$
\textrm{Var}[X] = \textrm{E}[X^2] - \left(\textrm{E}[X]\right)^2, \qquad \textrm {E}[X] = \dfrac{1+|S|}{2}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[X] & =\text{E}[{X}^{2}]-{(\text{E}[X])}^{2} \\  & =\frac{(|S|+1)(2|S|+1)}{6}-{(\frac{|S|+1}{2})}^{2} \\  & =\frac{(|S|+1)(2|S|+1)}{6}-\frac{(|S|+1)^{2}}{4} \\  & =\frac{2(|S|+1)(2|S|+1)}{12}-\frac{3(|S|+1)^{2}}{12} \\  & =\frac{(|S|+1)}{12}(2(2|S|+1)-3(|S|+1)) \\  & =\frac{(|S|+1)}{12}(4|S|+2-3|S|-3) \\  & =\frac{(|S|+1)}{12}(|S|-1) \\  & =\frac{(|S|+1)(|S|-1)}{12} \\  & =\frac{|S{|}^{2}-1}{12}\end{aligned}
$$

as required.

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[X] & =\text{E}[{X}^{2}]-{(\text{E}[X])}^{2} \\  & =\frac{(|S|+1)(2|S|+1)}{6}-{(\frac{|S|+1}{2})}^{2} \\  & =\frac{(|S|+1)(2|S|+1)}{6}-\frac{(|S|+1)^{2}}{4} \\  & =\frac{2(|S|+1)(2|S|+1)}{12}-\frac{3(|S|+1)^{2}}{12} \\  & =\frac{(|S|+1)}{12}(2(2|S|+1)-3(|S|+1)) \\  & =\frac{(|S|+1)}{12}(4|S|+2-3|S|-3) \\  & =\frac{(|S|+1)}{12}(|S|-1) \\  & =\frac{(|S|+1)(|S|-1)}{12} \\  & =\frac{|S{|}^{2}-1}{12}\end{aligned}
$$

as required.
